subject: chemistry
title: Theory vs Reality: Polarisation and Covalent Character
welcome_lead: Compare theoretical and experimental lattice enthalpies.
meta_desc: A-Level chemistry adventure on lattice enthalpy theory vs experiment.
final_note: You spotted covalent character hiding in ionic compounds.

concepts.def: Partial electron sharing in ionic bond.

walkthroughs.body_html:
If experimental LE > theoretical, compound has more covalent character. NaCl values agree well (mostly ionic).

AgCl experimental is more exothermic than theoretical: Ag+ has high polarising power leading to covalent character.

Small, highly charged cations (Al^3+, Mg^2+) polarise large anions (I-, S^2-) most.

Fajans' rules: covalent character grows with small cation, large anion, high cation charge.

AgI is much more covalent than AgF: I- is large and polarisable. AgI low solubility in water.

Anhydrous AlCl3 has covalent character; sublimes at 178 deg C, forms Al2Cl6 dimer with dative bonds.

mcqs.q: Larger experimental than theoretical LE suggests.
What state are the ions in when defining lattice enthalpy of formation?
options: ΔH becomes zero because the change cancels out.
The ions start as solid elements before being assembled into the lattice.
Gaseous ions — lattice enthalpy is the energy change when one mole of solid ionic compound forms from its constituent ions in the GAS phase.
The ions are in aqueous solution before forming the lattice.

mcqs.q: When water boils, what is broken?
options: The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken when water boils.
ΔH becomes zero because the change cancels out.
Intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are broken — the O-H covalent bonds stay intact.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.

mcqs.q: When you reverse a reaction in a Hess cycle, what happens to ΔH?
options: ΔH stays the same because it's the same reaction.
ΔH becomes zero because the change cancels out.
Its sign reverses — if the forward reaction is +100 kJ/mol, the reverse is -100 kJ/mol.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
